$comment: Canonical design tokens for Argentum. This file is the source; the dashboard's
CSS variables and the backend's Go report theme are generated from it by
`make tokens` and committed. Never hand-edit a generated file — CI diffs it.
Keys beginning with $ are documentation and are ignored by the generators.
`scope` decides which generators see a group:
all   → both the dashboard CSS and the Go report theme
web   → dashboard CSS only (chrome that has no meaning on paper)
print → Go report theme only (units the browser has no use for)
Colours are hex because hex is what a designer reads and what Go needs. The
CSS generator converts to the bare `H S% L%` triples shadcn/ui expects.
Light palette only: documents are printed and forwarded, so the dark palette
has no meaning on paper and stays hand-written in the dashboard's index.css.

$ramp: The neutral ramp is grey, not cream, as of T-U1. It was a warm cream
(#F5F5F0 ground, #E2E2DC rules) chosen when the product was a document
renderer with a dashboard attached. The dashboard is now the product, and
a warm ground tints every status colour that lands on it — an amber
'needs approval' chip on cream reads as decoration rather than as a state.
Ground, surface, ink and line are five rungs apart rather than three, which
is what lets a chat turn sit on a card, on a panel, on the page and still
read as three surfaces without a border on every one of them.
The brand red stays `primary`. It is the one warm value in the system and
it no longer has to compete with a warm ground for the eye.

background.doc: Page ground. Large fills, PDF page background.

surface.doc: Cards, table bands — anything that sits on the background.

surfaceMuted.doc: Hover fill and alternating table rows: one rung under the page.

surfaceSubtle.doc: Recessed ground: disabled controls, table header band, callout backgrounds.

surfaceInset.doc: An inset panel on a card — a trace body, an expanded tool call. Between surface and surfaceMuted so it recedes without becoming a hover state.

field.doc: Input and textarea fill. A filled field needs no border to read as editable, which is why it is a fill and not another line colour.

primary.doc: Brand accent. Rules, KPI emphasis, focus ring, chart series 1.

primaryForeground.doc: Text and icons on a primary fill.

primaryTint.doc: Primary at chip strength: a selected row, an active nav item. Solid rather than an alpha so it composites the same on every surface rung.

$ink: Every status colour has an `Ink` sibling, and the pair is not decoration.
A fill colour and a text colour are different jobs with different floors.
#F25C5C is 3.25:1 on white and #EF720C is 2.97:1 — both are fine as a
12px fill behind white glyphs, and both fail WCAG AA the moment they are
the sentence itself. The dashboard was already writing those sentences:
`text-emerald-600` on an executed proposal, `text-amber-700` on a pending
one, picked by eye out of Tailwind's ramp.
Each `Ink` is its own hue darkened until it clears 4.5:1 against all three
grounds it can land on — white surface, its own tint, and the page — with
the ratio recorded in its doc. Fill uses the base; text uses the ink; a

primaryInk.doc: Primary as text: a link, an active label. 5.50:1 on surface, 4.82:1 on primaryTint, 5.28:1 on background.

foreground.doc: Body text. Not #000 — a true black on a light ground is a contrast the eye reads as a shadow.

muted.doc: Secondary text: captions, footers, page numbers, chart axis labels.

mutedSubtle.doc: Tertiary text: placeholders, disabled labels, timestamps. Below the WCAG AA body floor by design — it never carries meaning on its own.

borderStrong.doc: The outline of something interactive: a control, a field, an overlay. One rung darker than border so a button edge is visible where a card edge should not be.

destructiveTint.doc: Destructive at chip strength: an error strip, a failed run.

destructiveInk.doc: Destructive as text: an error sentence, a failure reason. 5.28:1 on surface, 4.61:1 on destructiveTint, 5.06:1 on background.

$semantics: The three below say what a value means, not which series it is. They exist
because the report renderer was reaching into chart.palette for them —
`ChartPalette[7] // green` for a good KPI delta, `[2]` for a warning
callout — which made a categorical ramp carry semantic weight it never
agreed to. T-R3 proved the cost: the palette's green had to become an
azure to survive deuteranopia, and a good-news arrow would have turned
blue with it.
`positive` and `warning` became `all` in T-U1, which is the move this
note anticipated. The dashboard was stating those two ideas in raw
Tailwind — `amber-300/60` on the approval card, `emerald-600` on an
executed one — so the same two meanings had a second, undocumented
definition that no generator could see and no CI check could diff.
`info` stays print-only. On paper it is the neutral callout tone; on the
dashboard that role belongs to the surface ramp above, and a fourth status
colour nobody has a use for is a token that drifts.
Unlike the series palette, these are not required to be distinguishable
from each other under colour-vision deficiency: each one is drawn next to
a redundant cue that carries the meaning on its own — an ↑/↓ arrow, a
signed percentage, a callout title. Colour is the second encoding here,
not the only one.

positive.doc: Good news: a delta moving the way the reader wants, a `good` callout, an action that executed.

positiveTint.doc: Positive at chip strength: a succeeded run, an approved proposal.

positiveInk.doc: Positive as text: "Approved and sent." 5.07:1 on surface, 4.52:1 on positiveTint, 4.86:1 on background.

warning.doc: A caveat that is not an error: a `warn` callout, a proposal awaiting a decision.

warningTint.doc: Warning at chip strength: the approval card's ground.

warningInk.doc: Warning as text: "Approval needed". 5.42:1 on surface, 4.87:1 on warningTint, 5.20:1 on background.

info.doc: Neutral emphasis: an `info` callout, the default tone.

sidebarSurface.doc: Sidebar background — matches the chat composer, not the page cream.

sidebarForeground.doc: Sidebar text. The same ink as the page: a sidebar that whispers is a sidebar nobody navigates with.

sidebarAccentForeground.doc: Sidebar text on a hover fill.

$comment: One family, two roles — the dashboard has always used Space Grotesk for
both. `family` is the CSS name; `key` is the identifier the Go renderer
registers with maroto's font repository. Space Grotesk ships no italic
face, which is why there is no italic key: see fonts.go.

medium.doc: Table headers and labels. A separate maroto family because maroto's style set is normal/bold/italic only — there is no weight axis to put 500 on.

$comment: One radius. `rem` is what the browser uses; `mm` is the same 8px at 96dpi,
for rounded callouts and KPI cards in print.
8px, down from 12px in T-U1. There is still only one value here, and that
is the point: Tailwind derives `md` and `sm` as `calc(var(--radius) - 2px)`
and `- 4px`, so 8px publishes a 6px control and a 4px inner element for
free. A second radius token would be a second thing to keep in step with
this one.
Print units (pt), because this scale exists for the document renderer.
The dashboard's scale is Tailwind's and stays there: emitting pt-based
font sizes into CSS would be a unit error, not a shared token.

caption.doc: Footer, page numbers, chart axis labels, callout meta.

spacing.$comment: Millimetres, for page layout. The dashboard uses Tailwind's spacing scale.

sm.doc: Between a heading and its paragraph.

$comment: Page geometry. Not shared with the web, but it lives here so that a
margin change is one edit with a CI drift check behind it, the same as a
colour change. A4 because every customer of this product is outside the
United States; Letter would be the exception, not the default.

hairline.doc: Table rules and dividers. Below ~0.15mm a rule disappears on an office laser printer.

$comment: Categorical series palette for T-R3, ordered by series index: series 1 is
the brand red, and the order after that is chosen so a 2- or 3-series
chart gets the widest separation available.
Method: every entry sits on a rung of a CIE L* ladder spanning 24→82 with
a minimum pairwise gap of 6.8 L*. L* is the greyscale axis, so the ladder
is what makes the palette survive a black-and-white printer, and it is
also what carries a pair through deuteranopia when hue collapses. Hues are
then spread around the wheel so colour, not just lightness, does the work
for readers with normal vision.
Verified, not asserted: `pnpm --filter @argentum/design-tokens run palette`
prints the tightest pair in greyscale and under simulated deuteranopia and
protanopia (Brettel/Viénot/Mollon 1999, CIE76 ΔE*ab between the simulated
colours). `--check` fails below the floors — ΔL* 5 in greyscale, ΔE 12
under either deficiency. The tokens CI job runs it.
Why series 8 is an azure and not a green. It was #75AF4B, and the verifier
landed on it first: under deuteranopia it sits ΔE 5.0 from the brand red,
which is two series a red-green-deficient reader cannot separate at the
width of a chart line. A search over the whole HSL cube found no green at
any lightness that clears both floors against this palette — the warm
rungs (red 59.3, amber 73.9, brown 32.1) already spend the lightness a
green would need, because under deuteranopia every one of them collapses
onto the same yellow axis and only L* is left to tell them apart. So the
eighth series leaves the red-green axis entirely. #5CA8E0 clears greyscale
by 7.0 and both deficiencies by 24.8 and 31.8. Green did not lose to a
preference; it lost to arithmetic, and the arithmetic is reproducible.
Only `hex` and `doc` are read by the generator; `lStar` is recorded so a
future edit can see the ladder it is standing on.
Scope became `all` in T-U11. The dashboard had no charts at all when this
was written, so a ladder verified against greyscale and two colour-vision
deficiencies existed for the PDF alone; the moment the dashboard drew its
first series it would have picked colours by eye and disagreed with the
document rendering the same figures.
